title: What training do traffic controllers need in NSW?
description: NSW traffic control work training: the TCR, IMP and PWZ card classes, units of competency, the 2 year recency rule, penalties and TfNSW TCAWS duties.
shortAnswer: In New South Wales, anyone who directs traffic, implements a traffic management plan, or prepares or inspects one must complete SafeWork NSW approved training and hold a Traffic Control Work Training card for that class. Under the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2025 (NSW), a business must also confirm the worker trained in the last two years or has done that class of work in the last two years.
keyTakeaways: There are three classes of traffic control work in NSW: Traffic controller (TCR), Implement traffic control plans (IMP), and Prepare a work zone traffic management plan (PWZ). Each needs its own training and card class.
Training must be delivered and assessed by a SafeWork NSW authorized registered training organization, and applicants must be at least 17 years old.
The card has no published renewal cycle. Instead, a business must ensure the worker completed the training in the previous two years or has carried out that class of work in the previous two years.
Transport for NSW cites a penalty of up to $21,420 for a business that directs a worker to do traffic control work without the required certification.
Older IMP and PWZ unit versions remain approved courses only until September 1, 2027, so training records should show which unit versions a worker completed.
regulator: SafeWork NSW, administering traffic control work training under the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2025 (NSW); Transport for NSW (TfNSW) sets technical requirements through TS 05492:1.0 Traffic Control at Work Sites
appliesTo: Traffic controllers using a stop slow bat, boom gate or portable traffic control device on or next to public roads
Workers who set up, implement and remove work zone traffic management plans
People who design, vary or inspect traffic management plans and traffic guidance schemes
Construction, utilities, events, retail and logistics businesses whose workers stop traffic on a public road

sections.heading: Which law requires traffic control training in NSW?

blocks.text: The requirement comes from the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2025 (NSW), which SafeWork NSW administers. [Transport for NSW](https://www.transport.nsw.gov.au/operations/roads-and-waterways/business-and-industry/partners-and-suppliers/traffic-engineering-3) summarizes it this way: the Regulation "requires that all persons carrying out traffic control work must have successfully completed traffic control work training and hold a SafeWork NSW training card for the type of work they are performing".

The 2025 Regulation replaced the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2017, which was due for automatic repeal on September 1, 2025. [SafeWork NSW](https://www.safework.nsw.gov.au/legal-obligations/legislation/accordians/work-health-and-safety-regulation-2025) reports that the new Regulation commenced on August 22, 2025, largely continues the 2017 rules, inserts a definition of "class" for traffic control work, and adds provisions letting SafeWork NSW authorize training providers and courses. Traffic control work is a NSW specific scheme: it is not part of the model WHS high risk work licences covered in [high risk work licence requirements](/regulations/high-risk-work-licence-requirements).

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects SafeWork NSW and Transport for NSW guidance as at November 2026. The NSW legislation website could not be read directly for this page, so section numbers of the 2025 Regulation are not cited. Confirm provision numbers on legislation.nsw.gov.au before quoting them in a policy.

sections.heading: What are the three classes of traffic control work?

blocks.text: SafeWork NSW defines three classes, each tied to a different task, and each training course states what it does not qualify the person to do. A worker who needs to do more than one task needs more than one class on the card.

blocks.text: For IMP and PWZ, SafeWork NSW also lists the earlier E versions (RIIRIS301E, RIIWHS302E and RIICWD503E) as approved courses "until 1 September 2027 only", when delivered in line with the Standards for RTOs 2025. A card issued from those units remains a card, but training providers and buyers of training should plan the switch before that date.

sections.heading: Who needs a Traffic Control Work Training card?

blocks.text: Any worker who carries out traffic control work on or adjacent to a public road in NSW needs the card, whatever their industry. SafeWork NSW gives two examples outside road construction: a supermarket worker who stops traffic so a truck can reverse into a loading dock off a public road, and a construction site worker who stops traffic so trucks can enter and leave.

items: Exempt groups named by SafeWork NSW: school crossing supervisors, heavy vehicle inspectors, emergency services personnel, and Defence and Commonwealth employees.
Students with a valid Statement of Completion may do supervised work until they complete their final assessment.
To apply, a person must be at least 17 and have completed training and assessment with a SafeWork NSW authorized RTO. Online lookups are available through Verify NSW.

sections.heading: Does the card expire, and how often must training be refreshed?

blocks.text: SafeWork NSW publishes no expiry or renewal cycle for the card itself. The refresh requirement sits on the business instead. Transport for NSW states that a business must ensure anyone doing traffic control work has either completed the SafeWork NSW training in the previous two years for that class of work, or has been carrying out that class of work in the previous two years if the training is older.

In practice this is a recency test. A controller who works every week stays current on the card alone. A worker who last held a stop slow bat three years ago, and trained four years ago, cannot be directed to do it again until they retrain. Transport for NSW cites SafeWork NSW for a penalty of up to $21,420 for a business that directs a worker to do traffic control work without the required certification.

Because the evidence is a date of last activity, not a certificate date, the record most businesses lack is a log of when each worker last performed each class. That log is what an inspector would ask for when a card is more than two years old.

sections.heading: How does the Transport for NSW TCAWS standard affect training?

blocks.text: Transport for NSW published Technical Standard TS 05492:1.0 Traffic Control at Work Sites (TCAWS) on June 25, 2026, replacing the Issue 6.1 TCAWS Technical Manual. [TfNSW](https://www.transport.nsw.gov.au/operations/roads-and-waterways/business-and-industry/partners-and-suppliers/traffic-engineering-4-3) describes it as setting the minimum technical requirements for temporary traffic management on all public roads in NSW, and from July 1, 2026 section 77A of the Roads Act 1993 requires road work speed limit signs to be installed, maintained and removed in accordance with it.

The [TCAWS transition fact sheet](https://www.transport.nsw.gov.au/system/files/media/documents/2026/fact-sheet-ts-05492-tcaws-publication-update.pdf) says Section 9.5 Personnel outlines SafeWork NSW training requirements, clarifies the NSW position on the Austroads national temporary traffic management training framework, specifies worker roles and legal obligations, and adds fatigue risk management for temporary traffic management workers. TCAWS also covers roles outside the three card classes, including pilot vehicle operators, crash attenuator host vehicle drivers, and people operating portable traffic control devices.

sections.heading: Can interstate traffic controllers work in NSW?

blocks.text: Usually, yes. Traffic control work is in the Automatic Mutual Recognition scheme, so licensed workers from other states and territories, except Queensland, can work in NSW without a second licence. The licence must have been issued by a government licensing regulator, the worker must hold it currently in their home state, and they must notify SafeWork NSW before working. SafeWork NSW states that it "cannot accept Victorian training as issued by a Registered Training Organisation".

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each traffic control class as a separate credential attached to a role, with a recency rule based on the date of last activity rather than a fixed expiry, so a roster can be checked against both training and recent practice. The TCAWS Section 9.5 duties then sit alongside as site level knowledge points. See how this applies to [government and infrastructure programs](/industries/government-defence).

faqs.q: Can a TCR card holder set up a traffic management plan?
faqs.a: No. SafeWork NSW states the Traffic controller course does not qualify a participant to set up or work with traffic control plans. Setting out signs and devices to implement a plan needs the IMP class, and designing or varying a plan needs the PWZ class.

faqs.q: Can traffic control training be done with any RTO?
faqs.a: No. To get a SafeWork NSW Traffic Control Work Training card, training and assessment must be done by a SafeWork NSW approved training provider. A statement of attainment from an RTO that is not authorized for this purpose will not lead to a card.

faqs.q: Do traffic controllers on private property need a card?
faqs.a: SafeWork NSW makes the card mandatory for traffic control on or adjacent to public roads. Its examples, a loading dock and a construction site entrance, both involve stopping public road traffic. Traffic management wholly inside a private site is still covered by the general WHS duty to manage vehicle and pedestrian risks.

faqs.q: Does a Queensland traffic control ticket work in NSW?
faqs.a: Not under Automatic Mutual Recognition. SafeWork NSW says traffic control licences from all states and territories except Queensland can be used in NSW under AMR after notifying SafeWork NSW. A Queensland worker should check with SafeWork NSW before working.
